results.text:
That drive can weaken for reasons that aren't really my fault. I can get old, sick, depressed, or grieving, and I would hope the agape is deep enough that she sticks by me through some of that even if it puts strain on eros. But if I just get bored with life, stop having much of a life outside her, and make her responsible for nearly all my warmth, meaning, reassurance, and excitement, that's different. I don't get to be shocked if she wants me less.

If the eros does fade, maybe the agape is enough to keep us together. But *maybe* cuts both ways. If I tell her, “Even if I stop wanting you, I may still stay because I love you,” what exactly did I reassure her of? I may stay without wanting her. I may leave anyway. If she still wants me, both possibilities are awful.

Some couples do end up treasuring what they built more than the eros that got it started. Maybe that is enough for both people. Staying as a concession while the other person still wants you is different. That can feel terrible for both of you. At the wedding, how would either person know which future is coming?

results.text:
# Talk about making love before you do it

From here on, when I say making love, I'm talking about two people who care about each other deeply and feel super connected, using their bodies as part of that connection. If you’ve never experienced this, it may be like trying to explain the taste of an orange. If you don’t know what love is, you don’t know. That’s another conversation, and I'd suggest reading my inner child reparenting guide.

Having sex is just the physical act, whether that connection is there or not. But sometimes it can create the connection also.

Most couples do this backward. They start having sex and then try to talk honestly about sex. Now an honest answer might interrupt something that is already happening, so of course the conversation gets harder.

I want to know what she actually desires and what helps her body feel safe. Kinks? What flat-out doesn't work? What did her history teach her about her erotic wiring? What did mine teach me? Does sex mean recreation, bonding, sacred practice, stress relief, some mess of all those? I have to answer too.

And how often do we think we'll want it? That's not a very sexy question. But in a long relationship, one person is probably going to want more, less, or different sex for a while. That mismatch is one of the great factories of quiet resentment.

Maybe we don't know yet. Fine. Say that. *I don't know, but I'm willing to find out honestly with you.* I would rather hear that than pretend our bodies will handle the negotiation.

That's sexual compatibility too. Not only whether the bodies fit, but whether the people can tell the truth while maximally exposed. Before our clothes come off, let's find out whether we can do that. The conversation is already part of making love.

results.text:
## Can Casual Sex or a Situationship Actually Be Honest?

Your body doesn’t know that you picked someone up at a bar and agreed it was only for fun. Oxytocin, vasopressin, and the rest can start attaching you anyway. Then the next morning, you’re wondering why they didn’t call. Well, not getting pulled in any further is the best outcome still available, actually, since you just played Russian Roulette with a potential life bond to a stranger.

“I don’t know whether I want something serious with you. I’m not pretending I do. I’d still like to have sex.”

Okay. But sex can make a child. If this girl gets pregnant, she’s gonna call you. Then what? You block her? Agree to child support? Try to convince her to abort when she thinks abortion is killing her child? This is what penetrative sex can do. No contraception is perfect.

The STI part is easy: say what you know, or say you don’t know. Feelings aren’t. You can both mean it when you say this is only sex and still have one of you get attached afterward. If you’re both really numb or robotic about sex, maybe not.

results.text:
# Are you ready for the crucible?

I call relationship a crucible because I was thinking of Dr. David Schnarch’s Crucible Approach in [*Passionate Marriage*](https://www.crucible4points.com/books/passionate-marriage/). His focus was differentiation: remaining a distinct person while getting closer to your partner. He described emotionally committed relationships as “people-growing” crucibles. That was the part I recognized.

I didn’t know what a crucible was either. It’s basically a container where things get heated until they change.

That’s definitely what relationship does.

results.text:
[Inner-child reparenting](https://innerchild.u-dont-exist.com) is a big part of this. The present-day adult has to learn how to parent the child part instead of quietly hiring the partner for the job.

When that doesn't happen, I often see an adult expect the partner to know what they need without being told. They don't take responsibility for their own behavior, may barely notice the pattern, and deny it when somebody points it out. That's entitlement, whether they mean it that way or not.

Self-reflection is a good place to start, but it can’t see what it can’t see.

A peer can give another angle. Your partner is also usually trying to keep you, so they have an ulterior motive that a peer counselor hopefully does not.
